title: QASPA-MaxCut on Unweighted Graphs: Edge Encoding and QAOA Restarts
authors: Dmytro Sapozhnyk
abstract: Max-Cut is a common testbed for near-term quantum optimization because it has a simple Ising Hamiltonian, established classical baselines, and a parameterized quantum circuit whose performance depends on the outer classical optimizer. This paper develops QASPA-MaxCut, a shift-phase circuit for Max-Cut that encodes graph edges through controlled $R_y$ rotations of the form $\mathrm{CX}_{ij}R_y(θ_{ij})\mathrm{CX}_{ij}$. We derive the exact two-qubit algebra of the edge block, trace an unweighted four-vertex example, and compare one-layer QASPA-MaxCut with depth-one QAOA by exact state-vector simulation. The protocol uses seed 42, evaluates connected backbone-augmented random graphs with additional-edge probabilities $p_{\mathrm{edge}}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7\}$, and adds nineteen custom unweighted topologies. The QASPA-MaxCut score is reported after the algorithm's classical selection stage: the four leading QASPA bit strings are evaluated by the Max-Cut objective, and the best cut is retained. The QAOA score is the expected approximation ratio after local optimization, reported as a best-of-$k$ curve over one to ten restarts. In these small exact simulations, fixed-angle QASPA-MaxCut produces reported group-mean selection ratios between $0.955$ and $1.000$, the topology-level readout is unchanged in the retained finite-shot checks under the rule $\lceil 0.03047\cdot 2^n+1016.2\rceil$, and depth-one QAOA improves with additional classical restarts while remaining lower than the QASPA selection score in the reported mean summaries. This comparison motivates further study of the classical search budget needed to obtain competitive Max-Cut samples at shallow circuit depth.

infographic.key_insight: In small exact simulations, fixed-angle QASPA-MaxCut achieved group-mean selection ratios of 0.955–1.000, exceeding the reported depth-one QAOA mean expectation scores.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shallow Max-Cut performance depends on both circuit design and classical postprocessing or restart budgets, not circuit depth alone.
method: Encode graph edges with CX–Ry(θ)–CX shift-phase blocks.
Evaluate the four leading QASPA bit strings classically and retain the best cut.
Compare against locally optimized depth-one QAOA using one to ten restarts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Seed-42 exact state-vector tests covered backbone-augmented random graphs at four edge probabilities and 19 custom unweighted topologies; retained finite-shot checks left topology-level readouts unchanged.
infographic.watch_item: QASPA best-of-four selection and QAOA expected approximation ratio are different metrics, so the reported advantage does not establish superiority under matched sampling and classical-compute budgets.
infographic.paper_title: QASPA-MaxCut on Unweighted Graphs: Edge Encoding and QAOA Restarts

title: Bridging Pulse and Circuit Levels: A Geometric Framework for Deterministic Error Suppression
authors: Junkai Zeng, Hao Liang, Yong-Ju Hai, Xiu-Hao Deng
abstract: Quantum errors in noisy environments remain a major obstacle to advancing quantum information technology. Standard quantum error correction requires massive ancillary qubit overhead, motivating the need for hardware-efficient mitigation strategies. In this work, we propose a framework for dynamical quantum error correction at the circuit level, requiring no logical encoding or ancillary qubits. By extending a geometric framework (originally developed for creating dynamical error-correcting gates at the control pulse level) to the discrete dynamics of digital circuits, we map the accumulation of coherent errors to trajectories in a high-dimensional error space. We demonstrate that inserting deterministically optimized twirling gate sequences actively shapes these trajectories, utilizing destructive interference to keep the accumulated error bounded with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(1)$. This deterministic path-shaping suppresses circuit errors fundamentally differently than the stochastic random-walk behavior of standard randomized compiling with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$. Furthermore, we show that this circuit-level dynamical correction synergizes with pulse-level robust control, providing an analytical bridge between continuous noise dynamics and discrete quantum compilation. This research illuminates pathways to achieving highly noise-resistant quantum circuits prior to the era of fault tolerance.

infographic.key_insight: Deterministically optimized twirling gates shape coherent-error trajectories through destructive interference, keeping accumulated error bounded without logical encoding or ancillary qubits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework connects circuit compilation with pulse-level robust control to improve quantum hardware resilience before fault-tolerant operation.
method: Extend pulse-level error geometry to discrete quantum circuits.
Map coherent-error accumulation to trajectories in a high-dimensional error space.
Optimize twirling sequences to cancel errors and combine with robust control pulses.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports bounded O(1) accumulated-error scaling versus O(√N) for randomized compiling, but provides no hardware benchmarks or numerical evaluation details.
infographic.watch_item: Performance under realistic mixed noise and the implementation cost of optimized twirling sequences remain unspecified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Bridging Pulse and Circuit Levels: A Geometric Framework for Deterministic Error Suppression

title: A Variational Quantum Algorithm for Multi-Skill Project Scheduling
authors: Raul Martinez, Miguel Sánchez-Beato, Matilde Osa, Jorge Parra, Mario Calonge
abstract: Job scheduling is an NP-hard optimization problem with clear industrial relevance. In practice, distributing work across a team is not only about meeting deadlines or improving productivity; it also affects fatigue, stress, and employee well-being. Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) provide a promising way to address these problems through QUBO formulations, although their scalability on near-term NISQ hardware is still limited by Hilbert-space growth and barren plateaus. In this work, we simulate a VQA for a realistic Multi-Skill Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (MS-RCPSP), including worker capacities, skill matrices, task priorities, deadlines, and calendar stability during rescheduling. To keep the problem within a near-term circuit size, we use a temporal batch decomposition that solves one day at a time, propagates the remaining workload, and combines it with a logarithmic binary encoding that keeps every batch at or below 30 qubits. Because the ground state of a QUBO Hamiltonian is a computational basis state, entanglement is not required to represent the solution, raising the question of whether it helps or hinders ansatz training. We address this question by comparing the linear and brick-wall entangling topologies of a hardware-efficient ansatz with an entanglement-free reference that has the same number of parameters and by training every configuration with COBYLA and with Adam using SPSA gradient estimation. For the instance and initialization studied, the entanglement-free reference produced feasible schedules under both optimizers. With COBYLA, it produced the feasible schedule closest to the required workload at a fraction of the simulation cost of the entangled topologies, indicating that entanglement did not improve the solutions found by the VQA.

infographic.key_insight: For the scheduling instance and initialization studied, an entanglement-free variational quantum circuit found feasible schedules without benefiting from entangling gates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Day-by-day decomposition and compact binary encoding make skill-aware workforce scheduling tractable within simulated batches of at most 30 qubits.
method: Formulate multi-skill scheduling as a QUBO with worker capacities, priorities, deadlines, and rescheduling stability.
Solve one day at a time, propagating remaining workload with logarithmic binary encoding.
Compare linear and brick-wall entangling ansätze against a parameter-matched entanglement-free reference using COBYLA and Adam with SPSA gradients.
infographic.evidence_signal: In simulation, the entanglement-free reference yielded feasible schedules with both optimizers; with COBYLA, it came closest to the required workload at a fraction of the entangled circuits' simulation cost.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to the studied instance and initialization; broader scheduling performance and quantum-hardware advantage remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: A Variational Quantum Algorithm for Multi-Skill Project Scheduling

title: Symmetry-guided algorithms for variational quantum optimization
authors: Eunjin In, Kristina D. Launey, Darin C. Mumma, James A. Sauls
abstract: Quantum numbers associated with symmetries classify quantum states and identify the sectors relevant to a given simulation. Generic hardware-efficient ansatzes do not necessarily preserve the quantum numbers and may therefore explore states outside the target sector. We develop symmetry-guided algorithms based on the quantum-accessible Hilbert--Schmidt asymmetry (\(\AHS\)), which quantifies the deviation of a quantum state from invariance under a specified symmetry group. This quantity guides the optimization toward a highly reduced symmetry-based target sector, without enforcing the symmetry on the preparation circuit. We demonstrate the approach as a proof of principle in variational quantum eigensolver calculations targeting singlet ground states with collective SU(2) symmetry. The applications include a five-qubit \(S\)-wave \(p+{}^3\mathrm{He}\) two-cluster Hamiltonian, deduced from \textit{ab initio} many-body calculations, and collective spin models with up to 12 particles, which provide a many-particle benchmark of asymmetry-guided optimization. Across these applications, \(\AHS\)-based guidance increases the singlet probability. Overall, the proposed algorithms improve energy accuracy during optimization and ground-state fidelity compared with direct energy minimization, with substantial fidelity improvements in the larger spin systems. These results demonstrate the utility of an asymmetry objective determined by the group action, independently of the Hamiltonian energy, for improving the reliability of variational quantum optimization.

infographic.key_insight: Hilbert–Schmidt asymmetry can guide variational quantum optimization toward a target symmetry sector without requiring a symmetry-preserving preparation circuit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Symmetry-based guidance offers a way to improve variational eigensolver accuracy and reliability while retaining flexible circuit designs.
method: Quantify deviation from a specified symmetry using quantum-accessible Hilbert–Schmidt asymmetry.
Use the asymmetry objective to guide optimization toward the target sector alongside energy minimization.
Test singlet ground-state preparation under collective SU(2) symmetry.
infographic.evidence_signal: Proof-of-principle tests on a five-qubit nuclear two-cluster Hamiltonian and collective spin models with up to 12 particles increased singlet probability and improved energy accuracy and ground-state fidelity compared with direct energy minimization.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish hardware-noise robustness or the measurement overhead of asymmetry-guided optimization.
infographic.paper_title: Symmetry-guided algorithms for variational quantum optimization

title: Resource-efficient formulations of the Knapsack problem for quantum computing
authors: Pim van den Heuvel, Vrinda Mehta, Dennis Willsch, J. A. Montanez-Barrera, Kristel Michielsen
abstract: Quantum computing has emerged as a new tool for solving combinatorial optimization problems. Quantum optimization approaches usually operate on the subclass of Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems. Many optimization problems can be reformulated in this form, though there are often multiple ways to do so. The choice of formulation can considerably affect the performance of QUBO solvers in practice. In this work, we study QUBO formulations of the Knapsack problem, a canonical example of a problem with inequality constraints. In the standard formulation these constraints are converted into penalty terms, which requires additional slack variables. Here, we investigate three more resource-efficient approaches for formulating the Knapsack as a QUBO. The first two modify the standard formulation, either by deriving a smaller penalty constant or by reducing the number of slack variables. The third approach is a wholly different method, which avoids the use of slack variables entirely. All three approaches increase the probability of finding the optimal solution, both in simulations of the linear ramp Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (LR-QAOA) and on a D-Wave quantum annealer. The slackless method performs best, increasing success probabilities by several orders of magnitude even for relatively small problem sizes.

infographic.key_insight: Resource-efficient Knapsack QUBO formulations improve optimal-solution success rates, with a slackless approach delivering gains of several orders of magnitude.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Careful QUBO formulation can reduce auxiliary-variable requirements and improve quantum optimization performance without changing the underlying Knapsack problem.
method: Derive a smaller penalty constant for the standard formulation.
Reduce the number of auxiliary slack variables.
Use an alternative formulation that eliminates slack variables entirely.
infographic.evidence_signal: All three approaches increased optimal-solution probabilities in LR-QAOA simulations and on a D-Wave quantum annealer; the slackless method performed best, even on relatively small instances.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish whether these gains persist at larger scales or translate into end-to-end speedups over classical solvers.
infographic.paper_title: Resource-efficient formulations of the Knapsack problem for quantum computing

title: Band structure of two-dimensional graphene and of one-dimensional nanoribbons via variational quantum algorithms: from energies to wavefunction quality
authors: Raúl Medrano Millán, Rodrigo Gil-Merino y Rubio, Juan Borge, Unai Aseguinolaza Aguirreche
abstract: Simulating quantum many-body systems classically encounters exponential bottlenecks, which quantum devices circumvent by natively encoding wavefunctions. In the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, however, hardware noise constrains simulation accuracy. As a stepping stone toward strongly correlated materials, we compute the band structure of 2D monolayer graphene and 1D nanoribbons (zigzag and armchair) using a single variational workflow in the $p_z$ tight-binding approximation. Non-interacting ground states also provide essential initial reference states for subspace and warm-started variational methods to solve interacting spectra. By mapping the Bloch Hamiltonian to Pauli operators, we extract the ground band via the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and excited subbands via Variational Quantum Deflation (VQD), validating our approach from ideal simulations to execution on physical IBM Quantum processors. In ideal simulations, the workflow reproduces exact diagonalization results with high precision, whereas hardware noise introduces energy deviations of a few hundredths of the hopping parameter. While qubit counts scale logarithmically with ribbon width, fixed-depth ansatz accuracy degrades with Hilbert space dimension. Crucially, deepening the ansatz improves ideal simulation accuracy by over three orders of magnitude but worsens energy estimates under noise, proving that practical circuit depth is bounded by hardware noise rather than expressivity. Finally, we complement energy evaluations with a wavefunction-level diagnostic measuring subspace containment. This diagnostic captures degenerate manifolds and exposes optimization failure modes disguised by energy agreement alone. Operating directly on NISQ hardware, this validated workflow establishes a controlled baseline for studying topological and strongly correlated phases in realistic materials.

infographic.key_insight: Variational quantum algorithms reproduce graphene and nanoribbon bands in ideal simulations, but hardware noise limits useful circuit depth and energy agreement alone can mask wavefunction errors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow provides a hardware-tested baseline for materials simulation and reference-state preparation for future interacting-spectrum calculations.
method: Map graphene and nanoribbon Bloch Hamiltonians in the p_z tight-binding approximation to Pauli operators.
Use VQE for the ground band and VQD for excited subbands.
Validate against exact diagonalization and assess wavefunction quality through subspace containment.
infographic.evidence_signal: Ideal simulations closely match exact diagonalization; deeper ansätze improve ideal accuracy by over three orders of magnitude but worsen noisy energy estimates, with hardware deviations of a few hundredths of the hopping parameter.
infographic.watch_item: Logarithmic qubit scaling with ribbon width does not ensure accuracy: fixed-depth ansätze lose accuracy as Hilbert spaces grow, while deeper circuits amplify hardware noise.
infographic.paper_title: Band structure of two-dimensional graphene and of one-dimensional nanoribbons via variational quantum algorithms: from energies to wavefunction quality

title: Runtime Compilation for Quantum Circuits with PQF-Enabled $R_z$ Synthesis
authors: Siddharth Dangwal, Christopher Kang, Jad Habhab, Ritvik Sharma, Frederic T. Chong, Gokul Subramanian Ravi
abstract: In Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) using surface codes, reducing $T$-count is critical for efficient computation due to the high cost of $T$-state distillation. Probabilistic Quantum Circuit with Fallback (PQF) synthesis significantly lowers $T$-counts compared to standard protocols like Gridsynth, but introduces high circuit dynamism through extra gates inserted at runtime. This dynamism invalidates static compile-time routing, as these new $T$ gates require dynamic lattice surgery routing to establish non-intersecting ancilla paths to $T$-state factories while minimizing total execution time. To address this, we introduce $\text{R}^2$-PQF, a Runtime Routing protocol for PQF-synthesized quantum circuits. $\text{R}^2$-PQF dynamically routes gates layer-by-layer, computing paths during the execution of the previous logical timestep. To satisfy the strict computational window of $\sim t_{lattice\_surgery} + t_{reaction}$ and non-intersectionality constraints, we implement a Wavefront Breadth-First Search (W-BFS) and synthesise it on a 500MHz FPGA and 2 GHz ASIC. For a clock cycle of 2GHz, we achieve a median logical time-step of $1.51 μs$ for a 300 qubit Ising Hamiltonian circuit, demonstrating that $\text{R}^2$-PQF successfully resolves the vast majority of paths (with rare exceptions) within the execution window and enables the $T$-count benefits of PQF without latency penalties. Compared to a baseline stalling-based solution (the only no-runtime-recomputation solution), $\text{R}^2$-PQF speeds up circuit execution by $1.34\times$ on average and up to $1.76 \times$.

infographic.key_insight: R²-PQF enables the T-count savings of probabilistic quantum circuit synthesis by dynamically routing runtime-inserted gates with minimal latency impact.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hardware-accelerated runtime routing helps surface-code quantum computers accommodate dynamic circuits while reducing costly T-state demand.
method: Route gates layer by layer while the previous logical timestep executes.
Use Wavefront Breadth-First Search to find non-intersecting lattice-surgery paths to T-state factories.
Implement routing on a 500 MHz FPGA and a 2 GHz ASIC.

infographic.paper_title: Runtime Compilation for Quantum Circuits with PQF-Enabled $R_z$ Synthesis

title: On Revolutionizing Power Systems: Suitability of Quantum Computing-Ready Pipelines for Stochastic Unit Commitment Optimization
authors: Ying-Yi Hong, Dylan Josh Domingo Lopez
abstract: Modern unit commitment (UC) scenarios, particularly those involving uncertainties from demand fluctuations and renewable energy sources, pose significant challenges to traditional optimization methods due to the large search spaces they encompass. This paper proposes a quantum computing-ready optimization pipeline for deterministic and stochastic UC, integrating classical, quantum-inspired, quantum annealing, and hybrid quantum-classical solvers across test systems, including the IEEE 118-bus system. A novel Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) reformulation accommodates generator scaling and 24-hour scheduling horizons with compact Boolean logic penalties for startup, cooldown, and spinning reserve constraints. A divide-and-conquer strategy and Quantum Computing Monte Carlo (QCMC) simulation address scalability across 27,730 uncertainty scenarios, reducing compilation time by up to two orders of magnitude. Experimental results demonstrate the pipeline's ability to achieve efficient, scalable, and accurate UC optimization under uncertainty: the hybrid quantum method approach matches the classical baseline, reduces stochastic UC runtime from 40.76 to 14.79 hours, and characterizes pure quantum annealing as limited to small systems with 0.22% to 2.18% encoding errors and constraint violations. These results provide an analysis of the scalability and computational practicality of hybrid quantum optimization for generator scheduling in UC.

infographic.key_insight: A quantum-ready unit commitment pipeline matches a classical baseline using a hybrid quantum method while reducing stochastic scheduling runtime from 40.76 to 14.79 hours.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The pipeline offers a practical route to generator scheduling under demand and renewable uncertainty without relying solely on quantum hardware.

infographic.watch_item: Pure quantum annealing remains limited to small systems, with reported encoding errors of 0.22%–2.18% and constraint violations.
infographic.paper_title: On Revolutionizing Power Systems: Suitability of Quantum Computing-Ready Pipelines for Stochastic Unit Commitment Optimization

title: Improved Exact and Approximate Quantum Fourier Transforms from Multiplication
authors: Chandrima Kayal, Rajat Mittal, Manaswi Paraashar, Nitin Saurabh
abstract: In the world of quantum computing, quantum Fourier transform (QFT) has been one of the most important subroutines for quantum algorithms, as exemplified by Shor's factoring algorithms and phase estimation (which in itself has been used as a primitive in various quantum algorithms). In fact most of the well known quantum algorithms can be divided into two classes, QFT based algorithms and search based algorithms. The usual circuit for QFT (covered in almost every basic quantum algorithms course) needs $O(q^2)$ gates (and $O(q)$ qubits) to perform the exact Fourier transform over $\mathbb{F}_{2^q}$. Cleve and Watrous (FOCS 2000) improved this gate count to $O(q (\log q)^2 (\log \log q))$ using the integer multiplication algorithm in $O(n (\log n) (\log \log n))$ time for two $n$-bit integers (best known at that time). Our first main result shows that this gate count can be improved to $O(q (\log q))$. In fact, if there is a multiplication circuit, to multiply two $n$-bit integers, with $O(n (\log n)^α)$ gates; we get a QFT circuit with $O(q (\log q)^α)$ gates (improving upon $O(q (\log q)^{α+ 1})$) gates from the construction of Cleve and Watrous). Given the recent claim by OpenAI about integer multiplication, this opens up the possibility of having a QFT circuit with $o \left( q (\log q)\right)$ gates. On approximating the QFT over $\ZZ/(2^q \ZZ)$, the result of Ahokas, Cleve and Hales (ERATO 2003) showed that an approximating circuit can be built with $O \left( q (\log \log(q/\varepsilon))^{α+1} \right)$ gates, where $ε$ is the approximating parameter. Our second main result again improves this to $O \left( q (\log \log(q/\varepsilon))^α \right)$ gates.

infographic.key_insight: A tighter reduction from integer multiplication removes one logarithmic factor from prior exact and approximate quantum Fourier transform (QFT) gate bounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lower QFT gate counts could reduce circuit costs for phase estimation and Shor-style algorithms, though practical hardware benefits are not evaluated here.
method: Convert an O(n(log n)^α)-gate multiplication circuit into an O(q(log q)^α)-gate exact QFT circuit.
Obtain an O(q log q)-gate exact QFT construction, improving the cited O(q(log q)² log log q) bound.
Reduce approximate QFT complexity to O(q(log log(q/ε))^α) gates, removing one power from the previous bound.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical asymptotic gate-count improvements, not experimental benchmarks or hardware evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: Sub-O(q log q) exact QFT remains conditional on improved multiplication circuits; constants, gate-set requirements, and implementation overhead are not specified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Improved Exact and Approximate Quantum Fourier Transforms from Multiplication

title: Hardware Demonstration of Neural-Surrogated Quantum-Enhanced MCMC for Large-Scale Constrained Boltzmann Sampling
authors: Yuya Kawamata, Keisuke Fujii
abstract: Neural-surrogated quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo (QeMCMC) uses neural networks trained on samples from the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) to accelerate Boltzmann sampling. A divide-and-conquer strategy extends this approach to larger systems, but independently optimizing QAOA parameters for each subproblem is costly. In this paper, we develop a hardware-efficient implementation of neural-surrogated QeMCMC and demonstrate it using an IBM Quantum Heron r2 processor. Experiments with $N=144$ binary variables reveal faster autocorrelation decay for appropriate subproblem sizes while exposing challenges in neural-surrogate learning for larger blocks. We then extend the demonstration to a system with $N=1064$, where the autocorrelation decay rate per MCMC step is approximately $5.2$ and $12.3$ times those of global and local Kawasaki dynamics, respectively. These results demonstrate faster autocorrelation decay in a system exceeding one thousand variables using samples generated on quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Neural surrogates trained on quantum-hardware QAOA samples enabled faster autocorrelation decay in constrained Boltzmann sampling with more than 1,000 binary variables.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Divide-and-conquer sampling combines quantum-generated training data with neural proposals to apply quantum-enhanced MCMC to systems larger than individual quantum subproblems.
method: Generate QAOA samples on an IBM Quantum Heron r2 processor.
Train neural surrogates to propose moves for constrained Boltzmann sampling.
Use a divide-and-conquer strategy to handle larger systems.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments covered N=144 and N=1064; at N=1064, autocorrelation decay per MCMC step was approximately 5.2× and 12.3× faster than global and local Kawasaki dynamics, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Larger subproblem blocks challenged neural-surrogate learning, and faster decay per MCMC step does not establish an end-to-end runtime advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Hardware Demonstration of Neural-Surrogated Quantum-Enhanced MCMC for Large-Scale Constrained Boltzmann Sampling

title: Hybrid Quantum--Classical Pauli-Correlator Architecture for Image Reconstruction
authors: Sparsho Chakraborty, Siddhartha Patra
abstract: We introduce the Pauli-Correlator Autoencoder (PCAE), a hybrid quantum--classical architecture for image reconstruction. PCAE splits an image into patches and compresses each patch as a matrix product state (MPS). A small quantum circuit turns each compressed patch into a few measured numbers, and a classical neural network rebuilds the patch from these numbers and the patch position. A learnable energy term, taken from physics, is added to training and tracked as training proceeds. Two versions place the six qubits on a line (PCAE1D) or on a grid (PCAE2D). An averaging step makes the PCAE2D features follow rotations and reflections of the image exactly. Trained on one image at a time, PCAE2D rebuilds images from six public datasets with a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 25.8 to 41.6 decibels. On CIFAR-10 images not used in training, a formula-based stand-in for the PCAE2D features performs within 1 decibel of several simpler classical methods. Five trained models also run on real IBM quantum computers without retraining, and rebuild images at 25.90 to 31.52 decibels. A short argument and a synthetic test show that, with a linear final layer, measuring qubits in pairs is needed for targets built from products of inputs. These results show that PCAE works as a hybrid model that rebuilds varied images and runs on today's quantum hardware at the six-qubit scale.

infographic.key_insight: A six-qubit hybrid autoencoder combines quantum Pauli-correlator features with a classical decoder to reconstruct images and run on current IBM quantum hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Patchwise MPS compression enables small quantum circuits to process image data, while symmetry averaging makes PCAE2D features exactly equivariant to rotations and reflections.
method: Split images into patches and compress each patch as a matrix product state.
Extract measured features with six-qubit line or grid circuits, then decode using a classical network conditioned on patch position.
Train with a learnable physics-inspired energy term and symmetry-average PCAE2D features.
infographic.evidence_signal: Single-image training across six public datasets yielded 25.8–41.6 dB PSNR; five trained models transferred without retraining to IBM hardware and achieved 25.90–31.52 dB.

infographic.paper_title: Hybrid Quantum--Classical Pauli-Correlator Architecture for Image Reconstruction

title: Bounded decoding complexity in transversal circuits with magic state injection
authors: Lukas M. Sieberer, Giacomo Giudice
abstract: We characterize the complexity of space-time correlated decoding for fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures that implement Clifford gates transversally and realize non-Clifford gates via magic state injection. In this approach, decoding graphs for logical measurements are constructed by backpropagating measurement operators through the circuit, which causes them to grow with circuit volume. However, the decoding volume can be substantially reduced by decoding measurements sequentially, committing corrections, and excluding syndrome data that have already been processed for earlier measurements. For random circuits, we find that the resulting decoding volume associated with mid-circuit measurements approaches a stationary average that is determined by the density of magic state injections. Large decoding instances are exponentially suppressed. We further find that the decoding complexity is remarkably insensitive to different choices of measurement products to be decoded, and that the same qualitative behavior persists across different circuit connectivities and Clifford gate ensembles. These results suggest that scalable space-time correlated decoding of large-scale fault-tolerant quantum algorithms is achievable since the magic states that make transversal architectures universal also keep them decodable.

infographic.key_insight: Magic state injections enable universal computation in transversal architectures while keeping sequential decoding volumes statistically bounded in the random circuits studied.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Sequential decoding could make large-scale fault-tolerant quantum circuits more tractable by limiting how much space-time syndrome data each measurement requires.
method: Construct decoding graphs by backpropagating logical measurement operators through transversal Clifford circuits with magic state injection.
Decode measurements sequentially, commit corrections, and exclude previously processed syndrome data.
Compare decoding volumes across measurement products, circuit connectivities, and Clifford gate ensembles.
infographic.evidence_signal: For random circuits, mid-circuit decoding volumes approach a stationary average governed by injection density, with exponentially suppressed large instances and similar qualitative behavior across the tested circuit variations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract establishes decoding-volume behavior for random circuits, not end-to-end decoder runtime or accuracy on structured quantum algorithms.
infographic.paper_title: Bounded decoding complexity in transversal circuits with magic state injection

title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing Detection with Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks
authors: Alejandro Mayorga-Redondo, José Daniel Viqueira, Diego Alvarez-Estevez, Eduardo Mosqueira-Rey, Andrés Gómez
abstract: This work investigates the application of Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks to the binary classification of sleep-disordered breathing events in time-series data, aiming to distinguish between apneic and normal breathing episodes. A variational classical--quantum architecture is proposed and evaluated against classical Recurrent Neural Network models. Experiments were conducted on multiple real-world datasets with varying levels of complexity to assess the strengths and limitations of the quantum approach. In the comparative analysis, both classical and quantum models showed comparable performance. The quantum model achieved superior performance on the smallest dataset, while yielding slightly weaker results in the most complex setting. However, the quantum approach exhibited notable strengths, such as competitive performance despite a drastically reduced parameter count and low-qubit regime, as well as good generalization capabilities. These results suggest that, despite current hardware and algorithmic limitations, variational quantum recurrent models represent a promising alternative for time-series classification as Quantum Computing technologies continue to mature.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum recurrent neural networks matched classical recurrent models overall for sleep-disordered breathing detection while using far fewer parameters and few qubits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact quantum recurrent models offer a research direction for physiological time-series classification, though practical deployment advantages remain unproven.
method: Use a variational classical–quantum recurrent architecture.
Classify breathing time series as apneic or normal.
Compare against classical recurrent neural networks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multiple real-world datasets of varying complexity, the quantum model performed best on the smallest dataset but slightly worse in the most complex setting.
infographic.watch_item: Current quantum hardware and algorithmic limitations constrain practical use; fewer parameters do not establish a computational speedup.
infographic.paper_title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing Detection with Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks

title: Adaptive Qubit Encoding for Continuous-Variable Quantum Optimization
authors: Samuele Cavinato, Marco Tesoro, Gianluca Morettini, Marta Paiusco, Alessandro Scaggion, Simone Montangero
abstract: Optimizing continuous-variable functions on qubit-based quantum hardware requires a finite representation of the search space and a solver-compatible representation of the objective function. Fixed-grid discretizations provide a direct encoding, but restrict the search to a predefined range and resolution; at the same time, constructing a compact Hamiltonian for a general continuous-variable objective can be impractical. Here, we introduce a framework for continuous-variable optimization tailored to qubit-based quantum architectures. The method combines an adaptive discretization with an iterative local mapping of the objective function onto an effective spin-glass Hamiltonian. We assess the approach on unconstrained and constrained instances of the $n$-dimensional Gramacy-Lee benchmark, and on a proof-of-concept inverse-planning problem in intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) for cancer treatment. The results show that this framework can produce competitive solutions, supporting its use as a flexible mapping strategy for continuous-variable optimization in qubit-based quantum and quantum-inspired pipelines.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive discretization and local spin-glass mappings enable continuous-variable optimization within finite qubit representations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a flexible route for mapping continuous engineering objectives into qubit-based quantum and quantum-inspired optimization pipelines.
method: Adapt the discretization instead of relying on a fixed search grid.
Iteratively map the objective locally onto an effective spin-glass Hamiltonian.
Solve successive encoded optimization problems.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports competitive solutions on unconstrained and constrained n-dimensional Gramacy-Lee benchmarks and a proof-of-concept IMRT inverse-planning problem.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative runtime, qubit-resource, or quantum-advantage evidence, leaving practical scalability uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Qubit Encoding for Continuous-Variable Quantum Optimization

title: Conditional Quantum Priors for Chaotic Fluid Dynamics
authors: Shao-Bo Zhou, Yu-Ze Zhu, Hang Song, Xiang Zhao, Lin Yang, Xian-Min Jin
abstract: Neural networks that predict chaotic dynamics can reproduce short trajectories while misrepresenting statistics over long times. Quantum priors represent selected dynamical statistics through quantum generative models and provide statistical constraints for classical neural networks. Training a separate prior for each value of a system parameter, such as the Reynolds number, does not explicitly model how these statistics vary with that parameter. We learn a conditional quantum prior that approximates selected statistics of an invariant measure at unseen parameter values within the training range, without retraining. For Lorenz-63, the prior reduces mean Jensen-Shannon divergence by 56.9% relative to a classical multilayer perceptron with a comparable number of weights across 96 unseen parameter values. Across 101 values of the same parameter, the shared prior uses 84.7% fewer trainable weights than would be required by a separate quantum neural network at each value. We then use the learned prior to regularize classical neural networks, encouraging their autoregressive rollouts to better reproduce long-term statistics. For Kolmogorov flow at Reynolds number $Re=1000$, prior regularization reduces forecast mean squared error by 66.0% over 318 steps relative to the classical baseline without prior regularization. We also implement a photonic quantum prior for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, achieving a mean Jensen-Shannon divergence of $4.58\times10^{-3}$ for Lorenz-63 and $2.59\times10^{-3}$ for Kolmogorov flow at unseen parameter values.

infographic.key_insight: A conditional quantum prior learns parameter-dependent statistics of chaotic dynamics and regularizes classical predictors without retraining at unseen parameter values within the training range.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shared quantum priors could reduce parameter-specific model overhead while improving classical fluid predictors’ long-term statistical fidelity.
method: Condition a quantum generative prior on a system parameter to approximate selected invariant-measure statistics.
Use the learned prior to regularize classical neural-network autoregressive rollouts.
Implement a photonic quantum prior targeting NISQ devices.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 56.9% lower mean Jensen–Shannon divergence than a comparable-weight classical MLP across 96 unseen Lorenz-63 parameter values, and 66.0% lower 318-step forecast MSE for Kolmogorov flow at Re=1000 versus an unregularized classical baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization is demonstrated within the training parameter range; extrapolation and end-to-end quantum computational advantage are not established.
infographic.paper_title: Conditional Quantum Priors for Chaotic Fluid Dynamics

title: Classical training of conditional instantaneous quantum polynomial-time Born machines
authors: Oriol Balló-Gimbernat, Emiliano Tolotti, Laia Domingo, Fernando Vilariño, Adan Garriga
abstract: Instantaneous quantum polynomial-time (IQP) Born machines are attractive quantum generative models, as certain IQP circuit families are conjectured to be hard to sample, yet they can be trained classically. Previously proposed conditional IQP Born machines make the parameters of the diagonal layer condition dependent. We introduce conditional IQP Born machines, in which the condition is encoded in the input state and a single IQP unitary is shared across conditions. Efficient sampling and amplitude-ratio evaluation for the reference state entering the diagonal layer suffice to obtain unbiased classical estimates of a conditional maximum mean discrepancy objective and its gradients. We show that input conditioning can represent conditional families that no diagonally conditioned IQP model with the same number of qubits can reproduce. For the sixteen-qubit Curie-Weiss spin model, a single conditional model captures the magnetization transition at held-out temperatures. Its mean total variation distance is six times lower than that of diagonal conditioning under the same protocol and comparable to that of classical generative models with up to seven times as many parameters. We also train conditional models classically with up to 2048 qubits, which reproduce the mean squared magnetization of the target away from the crossover. These results extend classically trained IQP Born machines to conditional generation.

infographic.key_insight: Encoding conditions in input states lets a shared IQP Born machine represent conditional families inaccessible to diagonal conditioning at the same qubit count.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach enables classical training of conditional quantum generative models without requiring quantum hardware during optimization.
method: Encode each condition in the input state and share one IQP unitary across conditions.
Use efficient reference-state sampling and amplitude-ratio evaluation to estimate a conditional maximum mean discrepancy objective.
Train with unbiased classical estimates of the objective and its gradients.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the 16-qubit Curie–Weiss model, mean total variation distance was six times lower than diagonal conditioning at held-out temperatures; models up to 2048 qubits reproduced mean squared magnetization away from the crossover.
infographic.watch_item: Efficient training depends on tractable reference-state sampling and amplitude-ratio evaluation; the reported scaling does not establish quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Classical training of conditional instantaneous quantum polynomial-time Born machines

title: DynaMite: Dynamic Measurement Scheduling To Accelerate Fault-Tolerant Quantum Programs
authors: Dongwhee Kim, Suhas Vittal, Poulami Das
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers run millions of logical cycles to perform quantum error correction (QEC). As logical operations span entire logical cycles, the logical cycle time (LCT) dictates program runtime. Qubit measurements, critical to extract parity information for QEC, are the slowest operations and account for 43-86% of LCT. Measurement latencies impact fidelity: fast measurements lower our ability to correctly classify quantum states, whereas slow measurements increase the likelihood of decoherence. Hardware providers thus calibrate measurement latencies that maximize readout fidelity per qubit and use them to schedule all measurements during program execution. However, calibrated latencies are sub-optimal for logical performance because logical cycles span multiple QEC rounds, during which data qubits are not measured. This increases LCT and logical error rates (LERs) due to decoherence at the logical level. We propose DynaMite, a lightweight real-time measurement latency selection policy built on two key insights. First, logical cycles must use a measurement latency that is fast enough to reduce both LCT and LER for the QEC code, instead of the calibrated latency that only maximizes readout fidelity. Second, not all logical cycles are equal; many do not fully utilize the error budget of the QEC code, i.e., the number of failed parity checks it can tolerate without compromising LER. These cycles could use even faster measurements but do not, because latencies are chosen statically, whereas error information is only available at runtime. DynaMite exploits the fact that a logical cycle comprises multiple QEC rounds and selects the fastest latency for an upcoming round based on the error budget left and rounds remaining. Our evaluations show that DynaMite reduces LCT by 1.69x on average and up to 2.29x, and reduces LER to 0.46x on average and up to 0.13x of baseline.

infographic.key_insight: Adapting measurement latency to the remaining error budget and QEC rounds can shorten logical cycles while reducing logical errors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: DynaMite targets measurement bottlenecks that account for 43–86% of logical cycle time in fault-tolerant quantum computing.
method: Optimize measurement latency for logical performance rather than per-qubit readout fidelity alone.
Track the remaining error budget and QEC rounds during each logical cycle.
Select the fastest measurement latency for the upcoming round based on that runtime state.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports logical cycle speedups averaging 1.69× and reaching 2.29×, with logical error rates averaging 0.46× baseline and reaching as low as 0.13×.
infographic.watch_item: Practical deployment requires timely error-budget feedback and hardware support for changing measurement latency; the abstract does not quantify these implementation overheads.
infographic.paper_title: DynaMite: Dynamic Measurement Scheduling To Accelerate Fault-Tolerant Quantum Programs

title: Quantum Simulation of Electronic Structure using Quantum Density Functional Theory on a Programmable Integrated Photonic Circuit
authors: Giovanni Adriano, Akilan Rajamani, Francesco Hoch, Farrokh Labib, Nadja Z. Zaouri, Eugenio Caruccio
abstract: Quantum simulations of molecular electronic structure hold the potential for computational advantage but are inherently limited by the linear scaling of qubit requirements with respect to system size. Quantum Density Functional Theory (Q-DFT) addresses this constraint by reformulating the interacting many-body problem in terms of a non-interacting Kohn--Sham reference system. Here, we present and experimentally validate a Q-DFT algorithm that requires only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2(N))$ qubits to simulate a system of $N$ orbitals, thereby reducing resource overhead. More precisely, we solve the Kohn--Sham problem for the lithium hydride (LiH) molecule using the ensemble extension of the variational quantum eigensolver paradigm that minimizes the energy of the system in the subspace spanned by the ground and first excited states. To execute this task, we encode the problem with qubits on a quantum photonic platform, utilizing an architecture that combines a deterministic quantum dot single-photon source with a programmable integrated photonic circuit. By evaluating the molecular ground- and first excited-state properties, this work establishes a pathway for simulating larger molecular systems, demonstrating the viability of integrating qubit-efficient algorithms with advanced reconfigurable photonic hardware for near-term quantum chemistry applications.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum Density Functional Theory reduces the qubit requirement for an N-orbital Kohn–Sham simulation to O(log₂ N), with an experimental demonstration for lithium hydride.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Pairing qubit-efficient algorithms with programmable integrated photonics offers a route toward lower-resource quantum chemistry simulations.
method: Reformulate interacting electrons using a non-interacting Kohn–Sham reference system.
Use an ensemble variational quantum eigensolver over the ground- and first-excited-state subspace.
Execute on a programmable photonic circuit fed by a deterministic quantum-dot single-photon source.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experimental evaluation of LiH ground- and first-excited-state properties, but provides no numerical accuracy or hardware-performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Logarithmic qubit scaling does not establish comparable reductions in total computational cost or accuracy for larger molecules.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Simulation of Electronic Structure using Quantum Density Functional Theory on a Programmable Integrated Photonic Circuit

title: Data informed Ansatz Selection for Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Manav Seksaria, Advith Desu, Anil Prabhakar
abstract: Choosing a variational quantum circuit (VQC) usually means searching over ansatze and depths, and training each candidate. We give three rules that fix these choices from the data and the gate set alone, before any training. First, a circuit without entangling gates has a rank-one Fourier coefficient tensor on every subset of qubits. A singular value decomposition of a dataset's Fourier coefficients therefore indicates whether entanglement is needed, which qubits it connects, and a lower bound on the error of omitting it. Second, the rank of the quantum Fisher information matrix grows by $p_0$ per layer, after a first-layer deficit $d_0$, until it reaches a ceiling set by the dynamical Lie algebra. This law fixes the depth. Third, reading out all $2^N - 1$ Pauli-Z products from one batch of shots resolves half of the state's directions, the most any single-basis readout can. A single-qubit readout resolves an exponentially small fraction. For the Madelon dataset, the rules prescribe 7 blocks of 3 qubits at depth 3: a 239-parameter classifier with 78.5% test accuracy, found without a grid search. Ablations confirm three predicted effects: shallower circuits, smaller blocks and dropping reuploading all lower accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: Three data- and gate-informed rules select variational quantum circuit entanglement, depth and readout before training, avoiding an ansatz grid search.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach guides circuit architecture selection while exposing trade-offs in entanglement, parameter count and measurement information.
method: Use singular value decomposition of data Fourier coefficients to identify entanglement needs and bound the error from omitting it.
Choose depth from quantum Fisher information rank growth and its dynamical Lie algebra ceiling.
Read all 2^N − 1 Pauli-Z products from shared measurement shots to resolve half of the state's directions.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Madelon, the prescribed 7 three-qubit blocks at depth 3 yielded a 239-parameter classifier with 78.5% test accuracy; shallower circuits, smaller blocks and removing reuploading reduced accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Although Pauli-Z products share measurement shots, their number grows exponentially with qubit count, creating post-processing and finite-shot estimation concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Data informed Ansatz Selection for Variational Quantum Circuits

title: On the Hardness of Approximate Quantum Circuit Membership and Optimization
authors: Adam Husted Kjelstrøm, Jaco van de Pol, Andreas Pavlogiannis
abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is an indispensable component of the quantum software stack, used to reduce noise, maximize performance, alleviate costs of quantum error correction, or target specific hardware. A related problem is approximate membership: for a fixed set of unitaries $S$, decide whether a given circuit $C$ is within distance $\varepsilon$ of a unitary in $S$ under some metric $m$. Membership is a special case of optimization, where $S$ is a set of unitaries implementable at no cost (e.g., with noise-minimal circuits, or without magic states). Janzing, Wocjan, and Beth (Int. J. Quantum Inf., 2005) showed that, for the operator metric, the case $S=\{I\}$ (approximate identity) is QMA-complete when $C$ is promised to be either close to the identity or far from it. We generalize this setting in three directions: (i) promise-free inputs, (ii) besides $S=\{I\}$, sets $S$ containing only Clifford unitaries, or only generalized permutation matrices (i.e., no superposition), and (iii) the trace-based, spectral, and operator metrics. We show that, in all cases, approximate membership is PP-hard for wide ranges of $\varepsilon$, provided $C$'s gate-set can implement Clifford+T, as the gate-sets of standard hardware do. If $S=\{I\}$, or if $S$ contains only generalized permutation matrices, $I\in S$, and $m$ is a trace-based distance, PP-hardness holds for all non-trivial $\varepsilon$. If $S=\{I\}$ and $m$ is a trace-based distance, PP-hardness holds even for circuits over classical-reversible gate-sets. Our results indicate that approximate membership is harder over promise-free inputs than the QMA-complete promise version, and that this hardness persists across quantum resources (any gates, non-Clifford, superposition) and distance metrics. They directly imply PP-hardness of circuit optimization when minimizing total, non-Clifford, or superposition gate depth or count.

infographic.key_insight: Without an input promise, approximate quantum circuit membership is PP-hard across multiple target sets and distance metrics, implying PP-hardness of related circuit optimization tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results establish worst-case complexity barriers to minimizing total, non-Clifford, or superposition gate count and depth on hardware supporting Clifford+T.
method: Analyze promise-free membership near identity, Clifford-only sets, and generalized permutation sets.
Establish PP-hardness under trace-based, spectral, and operator metrics across broad approximation thresholds.
Extend trace-based identity hardness to circuits using only classical-reversible gates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical hardness proofs, including all non-trivial thresholds for specified trace-based cases, rather than empirical benchmarks or hardware evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: Worst-case PP-hardness does not rule out effective heuristics on practical circuits, and threshold coverage depends on the target set and metric.
infographic.paper_title: On the Hardness of Approximate Quantum Circuit Membership and Optimization
